I try to see every side of things, but I think I'm just like anyone when I admit I have my limits.

Knowing your own limits is the first step. Now armed with that knowledge you should be humble enough to always listen to other people's arguments and judge them on their own merits, not on how they relate to what you've already know before or your own personal feelings on the matter. If you do that simple thing you won't have to know all the facts yourself - you can count on others instead, even your enemies (sometimes especially them) to keep you informed.
I don't mean to be pedantic, but I ask in good faith if you will elaborate on this. You have my attention.

Once you admit you have your limits, then you logically are assuming that no one can know the whole truth of things. This logically implies that you need to work with others and the only way to work with others is to really listen to them and judge their own ideas and whatever they have to say in a neutral approach - untethered by your own preconceptions and biases. 50% of what people say is bullshit, 45% is worth listening to in the sense that if you do it long enough with patience and understanding you'll learn just a tiny bit of information worth keeping and 5% is really important and something you wouldn't have learned if you decided not to listen to anyone else but yourself and your close friends and family.

You never know who's gonna say those things to you - often they come from the most unexpected places, people you'd never normally talk to or even the people who disagree with you the most. That's just natural because they are the ones who live life most differently to you - and so they will have learned things you can't even imagine in your own life. But you can learn from them if you listen with an open heart.

We humans have a tendency to keep close to people who are similar to us: our neighbors, childhood friends, family... That's because it's safe - we know how things work with them, what they like and what they dislike, we know how to behave, how to respond to the things they say and do. We don't have to learn anything new, just be ourselves. This is not a bad thing, it's good because it's safe and we all need to have a safe harbor to rest and enjoy.

The very words we use are an example of that. For example: strange and stranger. Something strange is something we're not used to, we don't know or it's out of what we expect from our ordinary lives. A stranger is someone we don't know, possibly someone who lives in another part of the world - but does a stranger really need to be strange? All of our friends were strangers to us before they became good friends. Why are people so fast to say the strange and the strangers are "bad"?

If you live all of your life inside the safe harbor then you won't ever learn anything new - because it's always the same. If you want to learn, to grow, to explore you need to face the things that are new to you. Make new friends, learn new things, hear others about topics that you know nothing about... and while you're doing all of that keep an open mind that things that seem "strange" and "weird" at first can become good things once you get used to them. You always need to push your horizons a little bit and keep an open mind and open heart, otherwise you'll always be the same person you are. And that's fine, but it's even better to become a new, better person every day, just a little different from the day before. Of course don't go crazy into new things, but always be careful and take an interest on them.

Think of your favorite story. Think of your favorite hero. The only reason you love them is because something strange happened that forced this story to happen and this hero to get out of his normal life and get to know a larger world. If he had chosen to refuse that opportunity and stay in his own world and normal life he wouldn't have done anything worth reading/watching/listening about!
